Multiple testing

### The problem with multiple testing

Hawthorn can modestly lower blood pressure in people with pre-hypertension or mild hypertension

As a homeopathic medicine, which contains no active ingredients, it has no effect on blood pressure

population: 10 people with diagnosed high bp (average over 24hr)
two measurement: before taking hawthorn homo mu=145 s=1
difference
null hypothesis: Hawthorn homeopathy has no effect in blood pressure
therefore mean bp before and after taking hawthorn homeopathy is the same
t-test of change in bp
as expected no sig diff. p > 0.05

let's repeat the study again p>0.05
and again p > 0.05
and again p < 0.05 : a false positive (we declared it as sig, when we know it had no effect on bp, also called a type I error)

Let's do 100 experiments and plot the p-values of these in a histogram

5 false positive (or 5% if experiments give false positive results)

If the null hypothesis is true, 5% of your experiments will give a false positive.

### Two main methods to control for multiple testing

- The Holm method (published by Sture Holm in 1979)
    - Use when false positives are costly
        - Clinical trials, safety decisions, regulatory settings
        - A small number of pre-specified comparisons
        - Confirmatory / significance testing studies

- The Benjamini–Hochberg method (published in 1995)
    - Use when you're screening and can tolerate some false leads
        - Genomics, proteomics, neuroimaging (hundreds–thousands of tests)
        - Exploratory/discovery phase where follow-up validation will catch false positives
